paper_title: ProgramGym: Scaling Training Environments for Long-Horizon Program Reproduction Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Coding agents are increasingly used to build programs from scratch as software engineers do rather than to resolve issues within a repository or to generate a repository from a given requirements document. However, scalable verifiable training environments that force agents to discover what is required and to decide how the system should be designed remain scarce. Moreover, existing agent workflows also cannot sustain long-horizon development in which the agent explores the reference program before implementation. To address these challenges, we introduce ProgramGym, a framework consisting of Program-Env and Program-Agent for scalable training environments of long-horizon program reproduction agents. Specifically, Program-Env constructs verifiable training environments from repositories through a feedback-driven loop that repairs runtime sandbox builds and the quality of black-box tests. Using this novel pipeline, we obtain 1,648 training environments spanning C, C++, Go, and Rust. Program-Agent combines a role-isolated workflow of analysis, implementation, and review with revision management for compilation checks and failure recovery. Experiments on ProgramBench show that both Program-Env and Program-Agent improve performance on program reproduction. Fine-tuning on trajectories with these constructed environments raises the performance of Qwen3.8-27B from 34.87% to 42.84%. Program-Agent further raises the base and SFT models to 55.71% and 56.25%, both exceeding some flagship models. We will release the ProgramGym to support further research on coding agents that build programs from scratch.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Current coding agents (Qwen Team, 2026; Team et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2026a) typically handle issue-resolution tasks and repository generation tasks. Issue-resolution tasks such as SWE-bench give repository and an issue for the agent to patch (Jimenez et al., 2024; Rashid et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2026b; Shi et al., 2026). Repository generation tasks such as NL2Repo-Bench give requirements document for the agent to implement (Ding et al., 2025). In both settings, the agent starts from given codebase or specified feature. software engineer building program from scratch instead keeps asking what is required and how the system should be designed. To explore this from-scratch setting, program reproduction tasks such as ProgramBench ask an agent to rebuild programs observable behavior from its usage documentation and reference program without access to the source code or network (Yang et al., 2026b; Adamczewski et al., 2026). The agent needs to still discover remaining behavior by exploration and design the implementation from scratch. None of the models in the original ProgramBench evaluation fully solved task (Yang et al., 2026b)1. Training therefore requires interactive environments with reliable behavioral supervision, which issue-resolution resources such as SWE-Gym and SWE-smith do not provide (Pan et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2026a; Song et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a). MindForge (Chen et al., 2026b)is restricted to command-line programs and still leaves this supervision unverifiable. Building verifiable environments and using them over long horizons raises two challenges. (i) Scaling verifiable training environments. Building the reference executable and runtime sandbox requires accommodating repository-specific toolchains and dependencies. The black-box tests need to cover diverse functionality while rejecting incorrect reproductions, yet single test-generation attempt may miss important behaviors or produce weak assertions. (ii) Sustaining long-horizon development. General-purpose agent harnesses support tool use but do not by themselves keep exploration and implementation coordinated. An agent can begin implementing before sufficiently exploring the reference program and forget previously observed requirements as its context grows. Addressing these risks requires an explicit development workflow that preserves behavioral evidence and coordinates implementation, review, and revision. To overcome these challenges, we introduce ProgramGym consisting of Program-Env and Program-Agent for scalable training environments of long-horizon program reproduction agents. Specifically, Program-Env addresses environment construction by augmenting an existing agent harness with feedback-driven loops for runtime sandbox and black-box test construction. To produce the reference executable and its runtime sandbox, it separates online dependency preparation from offline compilation and returns build diagnostics to guide repairs. Test construction proceeds across functional modules in parallel, using program analysis to target unexplored behavior and validation feedback. The resulting environments provide reference executables, runtime sandboxes, documentation, and black-box behavioral test suites for training supervision. Program-Agent addresses long-horizon development through role-isolated iterative workflow of analysis, implementation, and review. It first records evidence from reference-program exploration and then alternates implementation with behavioral review in separate sessions. Persistent records carry requirements across rounds, while offline build checks and validated checkpoints support revision and failure recovery. Building on these designs, Program-Env scales 1,648 training environments covering C, C++, Go, and Rust. Each environment provides reference executable, runtime sandbox, usage documentation, and black-box tests, which are essential for training agents on program reproduction from scratch. We conduct extensive experiments on ProgramBench. With Program-Agent, Qwen3.8-27B reaches 55.71% Tests Passed and Qwen3.8-27B-SFT reaches 56.25%, both exceeding flagship Claude Opus 4.7. We further evaluate DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 under the same protocol. These results suggest that ProgramGym can scale training environments for coding agents that reproduce programs from scratch as software engineers do. We will release ProgramGym as scalable gym for the community to develop coding agents that discover requirements and design systems from scratch. In summary, our main contributions are threefold: We propose Program-Env, feedback-driven pipeline that builds the reference executable and runtime sandbox and constructs black-box tests from repositories (Section 4). 1Release-time results; later performance of the flagship models are at https://programbench.com.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Long-Horizon Program Reproduction. Training large language models as agents has gained substantial attention (Team et al., 2026; Qwen et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2024), with software engineering (SWE) emerging as promising application domain (Cao et al., 2026; Singh et al., 2025; Pan et al., 2024). Issue resolution is representative setting, in which SWE-bench tasks (Jimenez et al., 2024) and its variants evaluate coding-agents on addressing bug fixes or feature requests within given code base (Yang et al., 2026a; Shi et al., 2026; Ahmad et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026; La et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2024). Despite their growing diversity, issue resolution tasks depend on provided code base, while several prior and concurrent works go further by asking agents to code from scratch according to requirements document (Luo et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026b; 2025; Li et al., 2024). However, this setting typically relies on natural-language requirements document that prescribes the functional specification (Ding et al., 2025), reducing the task to implementation and leaving no room for requirement discovery or architectural design. In contrast, recent work on program reproduction from scratch requires agents to reconstruct the externally observable behavior of reference program from binary executable and documentation without prescribing implementation structure (Chen et al., 2026b; Yang et al., 2026b; Adamczewski et al., 2026). This setting therefore shifts the challenge from implementing specified repository to iteratively discovering what the program should do and deciding how to rebuild it, as experienced software engineers. Code Agent Environments Scaling. Existing program reproduction from scratch remains highly challenging (Yang et al., 2026b; Adamczewski et al., 2026). None of the flagship models in the original ProgramBench evaluation fully resolved any of the 200 tasks (Yang et al., 2026b). Due to the scarcity of training environments for such tasks, coding agents tend to be trained as code-edit assistants that favor localized bug fixes or single-file implementations with detailed human guidance rather than as autonomous software engineers (Adamczewski et al., 2026). Providing realistic and executable training environments at scale is essential. This strategy is already proven in issue resolution (Song et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026a), where generated environments improved SWE-agent performance (Jain et al., 2025; Pan et al., 2024). These frameworks still start from an existing codebase or well-specified task description. MindForge does not filter training trajectories by recovered program behavior, so functionally incorrect reproductions can still be treated as successful supervision (Chen et al., 2026b). By contrast, ProgramGym makes program reproduction from scratch training scalable by automatically turning repositories into verifiable training environments. This increases sample sizes and converts coding agents from compliant code editors into active software engineers.

sections.title: 3 PRELIMINARY
sections.content: Program Reproduction Task. Software engineering agents are increasingly expected to develop complete software systems with limited human supervision (Yang et al., 2026b). Issue-resolution tasks such as SWE-bench, however, start from an existing codebase and ask the agent to make localized changes (Jimenez et al., 2024). Program reproduction from scratch removes this implementation scaffold and poses more demanding task. Given only software program and its documentation, the agent must produce source code that recovers the programs functionality while independently making the software design decisions needed to architect (Yang et al., 2026b). Training agents on this task requires stable environments that support behavioral exploration and automatically assess candidate implementations. Each environment ei comprises an execute-only reference program built from Pi, its usage documentation Di, black-box behavioral test suite Ti, and network-isolated runtime sandbox Si in which the task agent operates. The agent can use any compiled language (e.g., C/C++, Golang, Rust, Java) and must provide source code and compile script that produces candidate executable program (cid:98)Bi. The test suite Ti compares the externally observable behavior of (cid:98)Bi and on selected inputs, and its outcomes form the basis for behavior-grounded feedback during training. Because Ti covers only finitely many inputs, passing it establishes agreement on the tested behaviors rather than complete semantic equivalence (Yang et al., 2026b). Scaling this construction across diverse repositories poses two challenges: (i) reliably building reference programs with unified pipeline despite variation in implementation languages, dependencies, and build procedures; and (ii) synthesizing finite black-box test suites with sufficient behavioral coverage and distinguishing faithful reproductions from incorrect ones.

sections.title: 4.2 EXECUTABLE AND SANDBOX GENERATION
sections.content: Program reproduction from scratch requires prepared runtime sandbox with the necessary toolchains and dependencies so that the agent can focus on rebuilding program functionality. To accommodate differences across repositories, Program-Env pipeline Φ uses Claude Code as the underlying agent harness and adds an outer loop that validates each proposed build procedure and provides the diagnostics feedback for revision. For each repository Pi with standalone executable target, the agent generates download.sh for online dependency preparation and compile.sh for offline compilation. The overall loop proceeds to the next stage only if both scripts succeed and ./executable passes loadability check. Otherwise, failure diagnostics are returned to the agent for revision. The validated executable serves as , and the prepared image provides the basis for the runtime sandbox Si. Further details are provided in Appendix B.2. Finally, once the build validation succeeds, the dispatcher prepares the resources for black-box test construction. It uses codebase size to determine the number of parallel branches and assigns each branch functional module. Alongside module assignment, it instruments the executable for coverage measurement and prepares the test runtime. It also extracts repository documentation such as README.md to form Di. These preparation steps run in parallel as detailed in Appendix B.3. 4.3 BLACK-BOX TESTS CONSTRUCTION Reliable verification is essential for effective supervision in agent training. For program reproduction tasks, black-box test suite Ti provides this supervision by comparing ˆBi against on shared inputs. However, tests generated in single attempt may cover too few behaviors or use assertions that fail to detect incorrect implementations. Program-Env therefore uses structured feedback to guide the agent in iteratively expanding test coverage and strengthening assertions. Following the dispatchers module assignments, test construction proceeds in parallel across branches. Each branch runs the Claude Code harness inside an outer loop that validates each delivered suite and returns diagnostics for revision. After each round, the pipeline organizes the feedback into three components, stored as structured documents in Feedback Docs/. (i) Summary records what was done and what remains unsolved and why, preserving context across rounds. (ii) Program analysis locates uncovered functionality with dynamic analysis and traces it to public entry points with static analysis. (iii) Validation screens tests through four checks: the pass check identifies tests that fail on ; the double check detects inconsistent outcomes across repeated runs; the dummy check identifies tests that accept dummy implementation; and the weak-assert check flags insufficient assertions. These checks help identify invalid, unstable, or insufficiently discriminative tests. In the next round, the agent reads these processed documents to repair flagged tests before extending coverage to unexplored targets. subagent terminates once its module reaches the functionality coverage threshold or the round limit. Once all branches terminate, their suites are merged and validated again, and Ti retains only the tests that pass all checks. Further details are provided in Appendix B.4.

sections.content: In long-horizon program reproduction, single-session workflows may lose early behavioral evidence due to context compression and consequently produce program that fails to compile (Anthropic, Inspired by the iterative workflow of software engi2025; Hao et al., 2026; Feng et al., 2026). neers, we propose Program-Agent built on Claude Code to support systematic development in long-horizon program reproduction. As illustrated in Figure 3, it combines an iterative role-isolated workflow (Section 5.1) with revision management mechanism (Section 5.2) for compilation validation and failure recovery.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Figure 3: Overview of Program-Agent. The Analysis stage explores the usage documentation and reference program to identify behavioral requirements. The Implement and Review stages then alternate to refine the candidate implementation for fixed loop budget. Handoff carries behavioral evidence and delivery reports across isolated sessions, Workspace maintains the evolving implementation, and Revisions preserves independently buildable source code for validation and recovery. 5.1 ROLE-ISOLATED ITERATIVE WORKFLOW Program-Agent adopts role-isolated and session-separated iterative paradigm. It decouples program reproduction into two logical roles (analyst and implementer) and three stages: Analysis, Implement, and Review. Each stage executes in an independent session to eliminate cross-stage memory contamination. Handoff artifacts carry behavioral evidence and stage reports across sessions without transferring the full conversation history. Analysis Stage. The analyst reads the documentation and explores the reference program, without editing Workspace, guaranteeing unbiased constraint collection. All extracted behavioral evidence and implementation guidelines are stored in analysis-initial/analysis.md and frozen as read-only reference for all downstream stages. Implement Stage. The implementer develops candidate programs in an isolated session based on frozen Handoff artifacts without accessing the reference program, to avoid context noise. The first iteration delivers buildable baseline to avoid fundamental compilation failures, while subsequent rounds incrementally resolve verified review issues. All implementation progress and code changes are documented in implementation-k/delivery.md for explicit traceability. Review Stage. The analyst compares the official reference program with the newly built, immutable candidate program, and converts all verified behavioral discrepancies into actionable revision requirements recorded in review-k/review.md. Strict read-only access is enforced on both the candidate program and the Workspace to prevent self-justifying modifications. Iteration budget. Given fixed budget of implementation rounds, Program-Agent executes one standardized Analysis stage followed by alternating Implement and Review iterations. This explicit iteration budget resolves two common issues in single-session workflows: premature termination with incomplete implementations, and unbounded low-value exploration that destabilizes long-horizon reproduction. 5.2 REVISION MANAGEMENT Across multiple Implement rounds, the shared Workspace can accumulate error edits until compile.sh no longer produces an executable. Program-Agent therefore treats independent compilation as the gate for each implementation round. It exports clean snapshot of the committed source and compiles that snapshot outside the development workspace. snapshot that produces an executable is archived in Revisions and forwarded to the next Review. sections.title: 6 EXPERIMENTS AND ANALYSIS
sections.content: This section presents an evaluation of ProgramGym. Our experiments are designed to answer the following four research questions. RQ1 (Effectiveness of ProgramGym) Does training on Program-Env and solving with Program-Agent improve program reproduction task? RQ2 (Training Environments Analysis) What scale and construction dynamics characterize the environments produced by Program-Env? RQ3 (Test-Time Scaling) Does additional Program-Agent iteration budget improve Tests Passed? RQ4 (Agent Behavior Analysis) How does ProgramGym influence agent behavior on program reproduction tasks? 6.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETTINGS Environment Statistic. Program-Env constructs 1,648 training environments spanning C, C++, Go, and Rust, using DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) as the underlying model. Figure 4 shows that the repositories fall into eight functional categories and that developer tools and CLI & system utilities are the two largest. Test construction uses 5,918 subagents across these repositories. Table 1 reports six black-box interaction categories. We then collect trajectories for subsequent training by rejection sampling DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) with Claude Code and filtering on test-case pass rate. Agent Scaffolds. To support interactive program reproduction from scratch, we use Claude Code rather than mini-SWE-agent as the single-session baseline. The task is long-horizon and often exceeds 256K maximum context window. Claude Code compresses context so the agent can continue, following the ProgramBench protocol of GLM-5.2 (GLM-5-Team et al., 2026). We compare it with Program-Agent using the same container resource limits. Program-Agent runs for up to K=5 iterations. Each task runs in an isolated container with 8 CPU cores, 16 GB of RAM, and 30 GB of storage, under an 8-hour wall-clock limit. Models and Training Details. We fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026) on framework (Zhao et al., 2024) and obthe collected trajectories with the ms-swift tain Qwen3.8-27B-SFT. We evaluate both checkpoints on ProgramBench and use DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 (DS-V4-Flash-0731) (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) to further assess our proposed Program-Agent across model backbones. More details are provided in Appendix D.1. Evaluation Metrics. We follow the evaluation metrics of ProgramBench (Yang et al., 2026b). % Tests Passed is the macro-average of per-task test pass rates. % Almost Resolved is the percentage of tasks with at least 95% of tests passing. % Resolved is the percentage of tasks that pass all tests without cheating flag.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: In this work, we used generative AI tools to implement methods in our experiments. ProgramEnv and Program-Agent use agent harnesses such as Claude Code to construct environments, generate tests, and collect trajectories, as described in Sections 4.2 and 4.3. Additionally, we used generative AI tools to edit the paper to improve readability. We reviewed all AI-assisted edits. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims, and artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI. REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT We document the materials needed to reconstruct ProgramGym. Repository collection, commit locking, and filtering strategies are specified in Section 4.1 and Appendix B.1. Executable and sandbox construction, including online preparation, offline compilation, and build-stage validation, are described in Section 4.2 and Appendix B.2. Dispatcher modules, coverage instrumentation, and test-generation sandboxes appear in Appendix B.3. Black-box test construction, the four validation checks, and the feedback loop are given in Section 4.3 and Appendix B.4. Program-Agents role-isolated workflow, isolation rules, and recovery checks are described in Section 5.1 and Appendix C. Training hyperparameters are listed in Appendix D.1. Evaluation uses ProgramBench with the metrics and container limits in the experimental settings. We will release ProgramGym, including environments, construction code, and training artifacts, to support reproduction.

sections.content: A FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS (FAQS) Why are there far fewer tasks than collected repositories? Two factors account for the gap between the 30,459 collected repositories and the 1,648 tasks. (i) Filtering. Many candidates cannot serve as black-box tasks because they fail to build on Linux, require display or user input devices, or exceed the 3,600-second limit for compilation or instrumentation, which we cannot leave unbounded. Such repositories are excluded before the test construction stage. (ii) Cost. Constructing an environment is expensive, about 82.99M tokens on average (Appendix B.5), so processing the full candidate pool was beyond our budget. The pipeline itself, however, is fully automated, so that the community can construct further high-quality environments from the remaining repositories. Why is the difficulty distribution skewed toward easy tasks? Under the complexity score ξ of Section B.3.1, the 1,648 tasks split into 1,492 easy, 151 medium, and 5 hard. This skew is intentional. (i) ξ measures repository size rather than the difficulty of program reproduction from scratch: large codebase may expose few black-box entry points and little observable behavior. (ii) Tasks far beyond current model capability yield almost no successful trajectories, so collecting more of them adds little effective training signal. (iii) Despite the skew, models trained on Program-Env show clear gains in program reproduction ability (Section 6). As model capability grows, the same pipeline can be scaled to medium and hard repositories to push the frontier of coding models further. Why not report mean coverage curve over iterations? We could not report mean coverage curve over iterations for two reasons. (i) Subagents terminate at different rounds, whether by reaching the coverage threshold, the round limit, or early stopping (Appendix B.4.3), so averaging over surviving modules would be biased toward the hardest ones and understate the gain from feedback. (ii) Coverage is only aggregated to the repository level after all branches terminate, so no repository-level curve over iterations exists. We therefore present case studies instead. The two cases in Figure 12 were chosen to represent the two effects of feedback, repairing weak tests and expanding functionality coverage. Why can the Implement stage of Program-Agent not access the reference program? This restriction follows the separation of responsibilities in software engineering: Analysis extracts behavioral requirements, Implement produces buildable source revision from Handoff artifacts, and Review independently identifies remaining discrepancies. If the Implement stage could access the reference program, the agent might continue probing and matching marginal edge cases after completing its primary objectives, delaying delivery and degrading the staged workflow into open-ended trial and error. Program-Agent instead delegates further behavioral exploration to Review, which converts verified discrepancies into explicit requirements for the next round. This design preserves clear stage boundaries while ensuring steady and auditable progress. Why do we not compare with MindForge? MindForge (Chen et al., 2026b) has not released its environments or trajectories. Without these artifacts, we cannot evaluate under matched protocol, so we do not report head-to-head comparison. PROGRAM-ENV DETAILS As illustrated in Figure 2, Program-Env is constructed through multi-stage pipeline, and this section provides the implementation details of each stage. We first describe how repositories are collected and filtered in Section B.1. Section B.2 then explains how each repository is built into validated executable and runtime sandbox Si. Building on these validated builds, Section B.3 presents the dispatcher, which transforms each built repository into the resources required for test generation through task decomposition, coverage instrumentation, test-generation sandbox construction, and documentation extraction, producing the test-generation sandbox test and documentation Di. Finally, Section B.4 details how parallel subagents iteratively construct, validate, and refine the final test suite Ti under execution, coverage, and program-analysis feedback.

The pipeline consists of Comprehensive Search, Metadata Validation, Commit Locking, and Build Config Detection. Comprehensive Search. For the corpus analyzed in this work, we search for repositories with C, C++, Go, or Rust as their primary language. Repository retrieval is conducted via the GitHub Search API. To circumvent its 1000-result limitation per query, we partition the search space independently for each language using six mutually exclusive star-count buckets: [200, 499], [500, 999], [1,000, 1,999], [2,000, 9,999], [10,000, 49,999], and [50,000, ). If query exceeds this limit, its star-count bucket is recursively bisected until the sub-query yields fewer than 1,000 results, the bucket can no longer be divided, or the maximum recursion depth of 12 is reached. For the openended highest bucket, the maximum star count observed in the returned results is used as temporary upper bound for computing the bisection midpoint, while the resulting upper sub-query remains open-ended. This search strategy stratifies repositories by programming language and star count, improving repository coverage within the constraints of the GitHub Search API. Additionally, we include fork:false and archived:false in every query to reduce duplicate and inactive repositories in the candidate pool. Metadata Validation. We locally re-validate the retrieved repository metadata to ensure consistency with the search criteria. Specifically, we check each repositorys primary language and star count, remove duplicate repositories based on full name, and require non-empty SPDX license identifier as basic metadata completeness criterion. We further exclude repositories already used by existing code-related benchmarks, thereby preventing repository-level overlap with prior evaluation sets. Commit Locking. Because GitHub repositories are continuously updated, we fix specific code version for each qualified repositoryspecifically, the latest commit (i.e., the branch tip) of the default branch at the moment of data retrieval. For each candidate repository, we extract the default branch field from the repository metadata collected in the first stage, query the head commit of that branch and record its SHA. Ultimately, exactly one commit is retained for each repository. Build Config Detection. After commit locking, we perform lightweight, static detection of the selected commit to identify repositories with explicit build-configuration evidence. For each repository, we resolve the root tree of the selected commit and retrieve its recursive file tree through the GitHub REST API. We then search both the repository root and its subdirectories for common buildconfiguration markers relevant to target languages, including Cargo.toml for Rust, go.mod for Go, and native build-system files such as CMakeLists.txt, Makefile, and meson.build for and C++. We additionally treat npm-related configuration, such as package.json, as auxiliary evidence of build infrastructure. repository passes this stage if at least one recognized marker is found anywhere in its retrieved file tree; otherwise, it is excluded. This procedure serves only as scalable proxy for the presence of build infrastructure and does not establish that repository can be successfully compiled. The final repository collection contains 30,459 repositories across C, C++, Go, and Rust. Detailed statistics for each stage of the collection pipeline are reported in Table 3.

Standard-library availability depends on the selected C++ language mode and library implementation. CMake 4.0 rejects cmake_minimum_required with VERSION 3.4 by default, because policy compatibility below 3.5 is no longer supported. In C++17 mode, libc++ omits std::auto_ptr and std::random_shuffle by default, causing compilation failure. Unstable features can change or be removed, making some projects dependent on dated nightly toolchain. Code enabling box_syntax fails with error E0557 on toolchains where that feature has been removed. C++ C++ Rust B.2 BUILD PROCEDURE DETAILS Online preparation and offline compile. Building project requires compiler, standard library, and build tools that match the project itself, and installing the latest version of each does not guarantee successful build. As Table 4 shows, the reasons language breaks under its newest toolchain differ case by case. The build environment must therefore be prepared according to each projects actual version requirements rather than fixed per language. To accommodate these differences, Program-Env equips the build agent with skill for each supported language that encodes how to resolve toolchain versions, obtain dependencies, and drive the build. Guided by the skill, the agent makes environment preparation explicit in script download.sh, which fetches and configures the required compiler, build tools, and third-party dependencies and exports the environment variables used by the subsequent build. second script, compile.sh, then builds the gold executable program within the prepared environment. The separation reflects the solving side, in which the source is reconstructed from interaction with the executable under no network access. Compiling offline verifies that the prepared environment is self-contained, sparing the solving model from generating missing dependencies or compilers. B.2.1 BUILD-STAGE VALIDATION Linter check. Validation combines static linter with two-stage execution. The linter, shown in Table 5, first ensures that the generated scripts do not mask failures, since hidden error leaves It rejects true, redirections that discard standard nothing for the build agent to diagnose. error, and placeholder content, and requires acceptable failures to be handled by explicit conditional branches. The checks are intentionally strict, as false positive costs single repair round while an undetected failure propagates to every downstream stage. The system first Execution check. Execution then proceeds online and offline. runs download.sh in container with network access, providing the script alone and not providing the project source, so that the script must generate its own dependency manifest for prefetching. Upon success, the system records the exported environment variables and snapshot of installed packages, and freezes the container state as the runtime sandbox Si. The system then places the project source in separate working directory, launches network-disabled container from Si, restores the recorded environment variables, and executes compile.sh. Since the build cannot reach the network, it succeeds only if the toolchain and local resources prepared in the first stage are sufficient. Validation checks the exit status of both scripts, the presence of an executable at the agreed location, and the format and linkage of that executable. As shown in Figure 2, the linkage check runs ldd on the to confirm that it was built successfully and no dynamic library is missing.

B.3 DISPATCHER DETAILS As Figure 11 shows, once the Executable and Sandbox Generation completes, the pipeline invokes the dispatcher, which converts the validated target program into the resources required for test generation and evaluation. The dispatcher comprises four components: task decomposition, coverage instrumentation, test generation sandbox construction, and docs extraction. Instrumentation depends on the runtime sandbox Si, and sandbox construction depends on the instrumented program. The remaining components are independent and run concurrently, reducing the dispatchers wall-clock time. B.3.1 TASK DECOMPOSITION Delegating an entire repository, often tens of thousands of lines, to single agent rarely yields test suite Ti with broad functional coverage, because the agent must simultaneously comprehend the codebase, prioritize among its functions, and remain within its context and generation budget. We therefore decompose the task. The dispatcher assigns module budget according to repository complexity. Let ℓ denote the number of production-code lines and the number of runtime dependencies. We quantify complexity as ξ = clip[0,10] (cid:0)log10 ℓ + log10(1 + r) 2(cid:1), (2) where clip[0,10] bounds the score to [0, 10]. Repositories are classified as easy (ξ < 2), medium (2 ξ < 4), or hard (ξ 4), receiving module budgets of 4, 6, and 8, respectively. Larger budgets induce finer-grained decomposition, leading to more focused generation and higher-quality test suites. decomposition agent then partitions the repository under this budget into modules, each pairing set of source paths with functional description. The decomposition agent is instructed to cover the principal production source, keep each module functionally cohesive, and avoid file-level overlap across modules. The agent further tags each module with the applicable black-box interaction categories in Table 7, and each subagent is prompted to target the behaviors in its tags. The distribution is shown in Table 1. If the repository ships native test suite under test/ or tests/, the dispatcher additionally appends test-reuse module that rewrites the suite into the delivery contract without consuming the module budget. TUI Keyboard navigation, key bindings, screen updates, and transitions between interaction modes. B.3.2 COVERAGE INSTRUMENTATION Overall strategy. To provide execution feedback to test generation, the dispatcher equips the target program with coverage collection, yielding the instrumented program. Rule-based instrumentation is the natural first choice, as it is deterministic and incurs no model cost. Build systems, however, vary considerably across repositories in their entry points, in how compiler flags are propagated, and in how source files map to build artifacts. language-specific rule therefore captures the common instrumentation path of its language but not the build behavior peculiar to each repository, and even determining whether rule applies to given repository is nontrivial. Moreover, injecting instrumentation flags indiscriminately may corrupt the build by conflicting with existing compiler or linker settings (Table 8, last column). We therefore adopt rule-first, agent-fallback strategy. The language-specific rule first constructs an instrumentation candidate, which an independent validator then checks for the presence of build artifacts and coverage metadata. Only upon validation failure does the system fall back to an instrumentation agent, an LLM agent that diagnoses and repairs the instrumentation. Language-specific rules. Table 8 summarizes the rule-based instrumentation method for each supported language (C, C++, Rust and Go), together with representative cases beyond rule-based instrumentation. These cases arise from repository-specific build behavior rather than from insufficiently detailed rules, so further refinement of the rules yields diminishing returns. Pairing languagespecific rules with the instrumentation agent is thus the more effective combination. First, provisioning each subagent with its own copy of the program and repository incurs substantial space overhead. Second, concurrent writes to coverage counters introduce race conditions. Shared artifacts with isolated state. The validated instrumented program, runtime libraries, and coverage metadata are frozen as artifacts shared within single pipeline attempt. B.3.4 DOCS EXTRACTION As shown in Figure 11, the dispatchers fourth component, Docs Extraction, employs an LLM agent to select two categories of content from the validated repository and place them into the documentation Di of the constructed environment. The first category is repository documents, namely the README and LICENSE. The second is test input assets that model cannot reasonably synthesize on its own, such as images and domain-specific binary formats, together with the minimal runtime dependencies they require. The agent records its selection in manifest, and the export copies only the listed files rather than auditing the whole repository. In addition, the pipeline rejects any sourcecode directory by rule. Together, these measures keep implementation details away from the solving side. B.4 TESTS CONSTRUCTION DETAILS The construction of Ti follows an iterative process of test generation, validation, and refinement. In each round, subagents generate and improve tests for their assigned modules based on feedback from the environment. Section B.4.1 describes how generated tests are validated to ensure the reliability of Ti. Section B.4.2 then details how feedback is constructed to guide subsequent rounds until the final test suite is obtained.

sections.content: B.4.1 VALIDATION FOR TEST CONSTRUCTION Validation for test construction ensures that the generated test suite Ti serves as reliable criterion for the external behavior of the gold executable program . Concretely, Ti must be faithful, passing on the reference implementation, stable, with results that do not drift under execution order, randomness, and effective, constraining program functionality rather than passing unconditionally. Four mutually independent checks, run in parallel, enforce these conditions. The pass and double checks establish faithfulness and stability, while the dummy and weak-assert checks establish effectiveness dynamically and statically. Pass check. Candidate tests are first executed on to verify that their expected results, input conditions, and invocation are consistent with the reference behavior. The system records the outcome of each test case and marks those that fail or error on the reference implementation for revision. With as the behavioral baseline, this check guarantees that Ti describes the actual behavior of the reference implementation. Double check. single pass on the reference implementation does not establish stability. The system therefore executes the same test set twice against the reference, isolating file state with separate working directories. The JUnit results of both runs are converted into normalized records containing the test identifier, its pass, fail, or skip status, and the corresponding diagnostic summary and output. If the two records disagree, the test is marked unstable and reported. This check prevents tests that pass by chance or depend on randomness from being accepted as stable criteria. Dummy check. Passing stably on the reference program still does not show that test constrains program behavior. The system therefore retains the same scripts and inputs but replaces the program under test with dummy implementation that produces no meaningful output, and executes the suite again. test that still passes is marked dummy pass. This check identifies tests that do not truly depend on the functionality under test, such as those asserting only process termination or tautological conditions. Weak-assert check. Runtime controls expose only extreme cases and say little about assertion strength. The system therefore audits each test with static linter of 37 rules (Tables 9 and 10), which rejects weak oracles such as sole exit-code checks or tautological assertions, assertions masked by conditionals or swallowed exceptions, access to the reference source, and nondeterministic dependencies such as network, time, or unseeded randomness. Findings are reported at two levels. Level Error Error Error Warning Warning Warning Warning Warning B.4.2 FEEDBACK FOR TEST GENERATION The raw observations available after round, namely execution logs, validation reports, and coverage data, have low information density. To guide the agent effectively, the pipeline processes them into structured feedback that answers three questions: which existing tests need repair, which uncovered code the next round should target, and through which public entries that code can be reached. Tests to repair are identified by the four checks, whereas new tests are guided by program analysis. Each round thus repairs first and then writes new tests. Under the guidance of feedback, effective and deterministic tests are written without blind exploration. Validation feedback and repair. After each round, the four checks of Section B.4.1 write their findings to validation.json. Rather than raw pytest output, each finding is reported as an actionable item with the test or script location, issue category, severity, diagnostics, and suggested fix, so that the agent knows not only what failed but also how to correct it. Repair precedes authoring for two reasons. First, repairing an existing test is far cheaper than writing new one, since the location and fix are already identified and the change is typically local. Second, newly written tests may introduce further issues, and without timely repair these defects accumulate across rounds. Repairing first keeps every retained test stable and effective, so that coverage grows on reliable foundation. Writing guided by dynamic program analysis. trustworthy verifier must cover as much functionality as possible, so the central question in writing new tests is which functionality remains unreached. Software engineering answers this with coverage, since unexecuted source locations largely correspond to unexplored functionality. C/C++ and Rust count executable source lines, whereas Go retains its native statement-weighted basic blocks. sections.content: Analysis isolation. Analysis runs in disposable copy of the initial Workspace. The executable originally present in the Workspace is excluded from this copy and replaced with an execute-only reference program. The session is instructed not to modify product source and may write persistent output only to its active Handoff directory. Once Analysis is complete, its disposable workspace is removed. Implementation isolation. Before the first Implement session starts, the reference executable is removed from all implementation-visible paths and retained only in root-owned private storage. Implement can therefore access the frozen analysis and review artifacts together with its own candidate, but cannot execute or inspect the reference program. It is the only stage that directly modifies product source in the shared Workspace. Review isolation. Each Review session runs in separate disposable workspace. This workspace contains snapshot of the current source tree, the initial analysis, all preceding reviews, the current implementation artifact, an execute-only copy of the reference program, and an immutable copy of the independently built candidate. The role may execute both programs through their documented interfaces but is instructed not to modify product source, build scripts, or version history. The entire review workspace is deleted after its artifact has been sealed. Artifact immutability. The Handoff root and all completed stage directories remain read-only during model execution. Only the subdirectory owned by the active stage is writable. After successful stage validation, the orchestrator transfers that directory to root ownership and recursively removes its write permissions. Downstream sessions may therefore consume completed artifacts but cannot alter the evidence, implementation reports, or requirements recorded by earlier stages. The /logs/agent directory is also read-only during model execution, preventing sessions from creating undeclared persistent state outside Handoff. Analysis and Review may create temporary fixtures in their disposable workspaces, but these fixtures are deleted with the workspace unless they are explicitly retained and documented in the active Handoff artifact. C.3 BUILD VALIDATION AND FAILURE RECOVERY stage is accepted only after both the model invocation and its stage-specific machine checks succeed. Analysis and Review must produce their required non-empty reports, whereas Implement must additionally satisfy source-state and independent-build requirements. These checks are summarized in Table 16. Table 16: Machine-checked stage completion conditions. Stage Analysis Implement Review Completion conditions analysis.md exists and is non-empty. delivery.md exists and is non-empty; tracked files contain no staged or unstaged changes; compile.sh is committed; and clean source snapshot independently produces an executable. review.md exists and is non-empty. Source-state validation. After an Implement session terminates, the orchestrator verifies that delivery.md is non-empty, no tracked file has staged or unstaged changes, and compile.sh is tracked by Git. The current Git HEAD is then recorded as the source revision for the round. Untracked files do not directly fail this check, although the role contract requires all intended source files to be committed and generated artifacts to be ignored. Independent build. The orchestrator exports clean Git archive of the validated source revision into new build directory rather than compiling directly in the development Workspace. It removes common HTTP proxy, Python package index, and npm registry variables before running compile.sh with 300-second timeout. build is successful only if the script terminates successfully and produces file named executable.

The same record is copied to the current implementation artifact as independent-build.json. The resulting executable is then used as the immutable candidate for Review, while the committed source tree and compile.sh remain the primary task deliverable. Bounded retry. Each stage has an independent attempt budget, configurable from one to three attempts and set to two by default. Every retry starts fresh model session. The new session receives only bounded diagnostic describing the previous delivery or build failure, rather than the previous transcript. When Analysis or Review fails validation, its stage directory is deleted before the next attempt. When Implement or its independent build fails, Program-Agent also deletes the current build snapshot, resets the Workspace to the commit captured at the beginning of the round, and removes newly generated untracked files. Reusable Go caches are excluded from this cleanup. Build stdout and stderr from failed attempts are retained privately for diagnosis. Last-stable recovery. Every independently built revision becomes the new last-stable state, which contains both its source commit and matching executable. On normal completion or after later error or timeout, Program-Agent resets the Workspace to the last-stable source commit and restores its executable. If no implementation round ever passes independent build validation, any residual executable is removed so that an unvalidated intermediate candidate cannot be evaluated.

sections.content: D.1 TRAINING DETAILS We fine-tune Qwen3.8-27B on trajectories collected from Program-Env for two epochs using msswift (Zhao et al., 2024). We issue task-level rollout requests for all 1,648 Program-Env tasks. Because Claude Code resets or switches its conversation context during rollout, single task-level rollout can yield multiple interaction segments with separate contexts. We treat each such segment as separate training trajectory for supervised fine-tuning, yielding 64,505 training trajectories in total. sections.content: We pack training sequences into blocks of up to 262,144 tokens to accommodate long interaction trajectories. Examples exceeding the maximum sequence length are discarded. We compute the training loss only over eligible model-generated assistant tokens, while user inputs, environment feedback, and tool observations are used as conditioning context and excluded from the loss. Within assistant outputs, we additionally set the loss mask to zero for assistant turns that invoke tools unavailable in the corresponding environment. These invalid tool-use actions therefore do not contribute to the training objective, while the remaining valid turns from the same trajectory are retained. Training uses BF16 precision with full activation recomputation to reduce memory usage. D.3 EXTRA ANALYSIS OF AGENT BEHAVIOR Figure 21: Cumulative distribution of test pass rates across models and agent scaffolds on ProgramBench. Structured iteration shifts the full distribution of solution quality. Figure 21 shows that Program-Agent improves not just average results, but also how test pass rates are distributed across different tasks. When using Qwen3.8-27B, it increases the share of tasks that pass at least 50% of tests from 40.5% to 62.0%, and raises the share passing at least 75% of tests from 18.0% to 34.0%. With Qwen3.8-27B-SFT, the corresponding gains are from 43.5% to 62.0% and from 9.5% to 29.5%. The two Program-Agent curves stay close over most of the threshold range. This tells us its structured workflow with separate roles delivers more steady benefits, compared to simply switching between these two model versions. On the other hand, the effect of SFT changes depending on which test threshold we look at. SFT helps more tasks reach partial working functionality, but it cannot reliably boost the high-fidelity cases at the upper end of the distribution. The slow falling shape of all four curves also shows that tasks vary widely in difficulty. Meanwhile, the upward shift caused by Program-Agent demonstrates that this iterative development method works well across wider range of task difficulty levels. Behavioral fidelity does not require reproducing the full reference codebase. To compare implementations that have roughly the same functions, we limit our code-size analysis to solutions that pass at least 75% of the behavior tests. This gives us 182 test runs covering 93 tasks and four different modelagent setups. As shown in Figure 22, these generated solutions have median of 1,881 lines of code, while the matching reference implementations have 2,596 lines. In total, 67.6% of the test runs sit below the = parity line, and the median ratio of model-generated code lines to reference code lines is 0.64. The implementations that exceed parity mostly come from smaller projects: their reference code has median of 969 lines, while cases below parity have reference code with median of 4,303 lines. This pattern tied to project size shows that small tasks are more impacted by fixed setup code and extra compatibility code. For large tasks, by contrast, agents can often recreate the required features just by coding the behavior visible through program interfaces and tests. Program-Agent trades compactness for more elaborate implementations. Figure 23 shows that the median code size for all four configurations stays below the parity level, but their distributions are quite different. When using Qwen3.8-27B, Program-Agent increases the median LoC ratio from 0.58 to 0.75, and when using Qwen3.8-27B-SFT, it raises the ratio from 0.49 to 0.67.

sections.content: Figure 22: Reference vs. model code lines on loglog scale. The = diagonal indicates parity. Only solutions passing 75% of tests are shown. Figure 23: LoC ratio (model / reference) by modelagent configuration for solutions passing 75% of tests. The dashed line marks parity. Figure 24: LoC ratio (model / reference) by reference language for solutions passing 75% of tests. Its upper quartile values also hit 1.53 and 1.36. By comparison, the matching Claude Code configurations only reach 1.01 and 0.75. This means Program-Agent achieves better functional performance not just by producing shorter code uniformly. Its iterative process often builds more complete and detailed implementations, and sometimes the generated code becomes larger than the reference version. When combined with the test-pass distributions shown in Figure 21, this finding indicates the extra code comes from repeated tries to handle behaviors that the first version of code fails to cover. Still, how large these final solutions end up varies lot between different tasks. Reference-language ecosystems shape reproduction compactness. Figure 24 shows clear trend that changes with programming language. C/C++ tasks have the lowest median ratio of 0.39, and only 13.3% of the generated implementations meet or exceed the reference code size. Go falls in the middle with median ratio of 0.55, while Rust is closest to the reference code size, with median ratio of 0.72 and 35.5% of generated solutions meeting or exceeding the reference size. One reasonable explanation is that agents can often recreate the functions of C/C++ utilities using more concise abstract code, without rebuilding all the low-level underlying code present in fully developed reference projects. On the other hand, Rust tasks are more commonly reimplemented using Rust code with similar structure, so the new code keeps much of the verbosity seen in the original reference code. The long upper tails for Go and Rust in the figure also tell us that some tasks require large amounts of extra code to handle compatibility or embed behavioral data, which makes the rebuilt implementation far longer than the original reference code.
